The Pacific longnose parrotfish Hipposcarus longiceps is a demersal spawner that inhabits Indo-Pacific coral reef systems, where water temperatures are relatively stable throughout the year. Under the prevailing thermal conditions typical of its range, approximately 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], this species exhibits a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 12% [GSI = 12%]. The species' maximum recorded total length, or ultimate total length, is 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], a size that places it among the larger members of the Scarinae subfamily that graze the epilithic algal matrix of coral reefs.

Females of this species initiate the maturation of their gonads and attain sexual maturity once they surpass a total length of 32.9 cm [Lp = 32.9 cm], a length-at-puberty that corresponds to a wet weight of 449 grams [Wwp = 449 grams] as estimated from the length-weight relationship. This reproductive threshold represents a significant developmental milestone in the species' life history, as individuals below this size do not participate in spawning aggregations. The relationship between body length and mass in Hipposcarus longiceps follows an allometric scaling pattern similar to that observed in related scarine labrids, and the mass associated with the pubertal length is considerably intermediate between the neonatal mass and the asymptotic body mass. Adult fish that have surpassed this size threshold can be found in mixed-sex foraging groups on the reef flat and slope, and they exhibit the characteristic fused beak-like dentition used for scraping algae from carbonate substrates.

The early life stages of Hipposcarus longiceps begin with a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.00023 grams [Wwb = 0.00023 grams], a value consistent with the tiny pelagic eggs that are released during broadcast spawning events. This minuscule mass, calculated based on an egg diameter of approximately 0.75 millimeters as seen in related chaetodontid species, reflects the substantial energetic dilution inherent in producing large numbers of offspring. The fertilised ova are released into the water column, where they undergo embryogenesis as buoyant, transparent chorionate embryos before hatching into yolk-sac larvae. The resulting planktonic teleost larvae then embark on an extended pelagic phase, subsisting on endogenous yolk reserves until the onset of exogenous feeding. This lecithotrophic larval stage is followed by a period of rapid growth and morphological transformation as the larvae approach metamorphosis and benthic settlement onto suitable coral rubble or seagrass habitats.

As these fish continue to develop and grow, they eventually approach the asymptotic body size characteristic of the species, with an ultimate wet weight of 2755 grams [Wwi = 2755 grams] recorded for fully grown adults. This substantial body mass is reached after several years of feeding on filamentous algae and detritus, and it represents the upper bound of the size distribution observed in wild populations. The corresponding ultimate total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm] is rarely exceeded even among the oldest individuals, indicating a determinate or near-determinate growth pattern once the asymptotic size is approached. Gravid individuals at this size are considered to be at their peak reproductive capacity, contributing a disproportionately large share of the annual egg production to the reef ecosystem. The large body size also confers advantages in predator avoidance and territory defense, allowing these dominant parrotfish to maintain exclusive feeding areas on the reef.

The species' maximum lifespan has been estimated at approximately 4015 days [am = approximately 4015 days] based on studies conducted at the ambient reef temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. The gonadosomatic index was 12% [GSI = 12%] at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. Over the course of this extended period, individuals undergo a pronounced ontogenetic shift in coloration and social status, with terminal-phase males emerging from large female individuals through a process of protogynous sex change. The reproductive and somatic investment strategies across these eleven years must balance the energetic demands of daily foraging, predator avoidance, and the production of pelagic eggs during the three annual spawning events. Senescent individuals near the end of their lifespan exhibit reduced body condition and diminished spawning success.
